newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish suppliers worried as Tesco buys Quinnsworth.
newsitem.headline: Irish suppliers worried as Tesco buys Quinnsworth.

text.p: Irish suppliers said on Friday that they were concerned by news that British supermarket group Tesco Plc had acquired Associated British Foods' Quinnsworth and Crazy Prices chain in the Republic of Ireland.

"Any change of ownership of a company which controls 26 percent of the Irish grocery market will obviously be treated seriously by the food, drink and tobacco sector," Ciaran Fitzgerald, director of the Irish Food, Drink and Tobacco Federation said in a statement.

Ireland's Small Firms Association (SFA) also expressed alarm at the takeover and said it could sound the death knell for many small Irish suppliers who currently supply over 750 million Irish pounds of products annually to the group.
Earlier, Tesco said it had agreed to buy the ABF's food retailing and related businesses in the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland for 630 million pounds.
The SFA said job losses could follow the takeover as Irish suppliers would face a double hit.

If they maintained business with the new owners it would almost certainly be at lower payment levels and longer credit periods while small Irish suppliers would not be able to compete in an open tendering process for Tesco's own brand products with large UK-based suppliers.
The Food, Drink and Tobacco Federation noted that supermarket own-labels account for around 15 percent of the market in Ireland but the figure in Britain is closer to 50 percent.
"If we take Tesco as an example, trading in the UK market, the Tesco brand accounts for almost half of the total Tesco business," the Federation said.

"From the Irish suppliers' point of view this raises the question as to where this brand will be sourced. It is logical to assume that, given longstanding arrangements with their UK suppliers that Tesco will continue to source its Tesco brand for the Irish market from UK suppliers," it said.

The Irish grocery market is worth around four billion Irish pounds with 45,000 people employed in manufacturing, a further 10,000 in distribution and an additional 90,000 in the retail and wholesale sector.

It underpins the whole food and drink sector which is the most important manufacturing sector in the Irish economy, accounting for 24 percent of manufacturing employment and 30 percent of manufacturing turnover.
